opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the core idea is to treat the weights of trained neural networks as a data modality in their own right. Instead of images or text, our training samples are the parameters of other models.

The first step is building what we call a model zoo: a large, systematically generated population of models. We train many networks of the same architecture on a task while varying things like the random seed, initialization, hyperparameters, and sometimes the dataset. We also save checkpoints along the training trajectory, so we capture models at different stages, not just the final ones. That gives us a structured, diverse dataset where we know the provenance of every sample.

Then there's the question of representation. You can flatten all the weights into a long vector, but that ignores important structure. A big one is permutation symmetry: you can shuffle the neurons in a hidden layer, adjust the connecting weights accordingly, and get a functionally identical network with a completely different weight vector. So we either align models to a canonical form before training, or use augmentations that exploit these symmetries, which also turns out to be a very effective form of data augmentation for self-supervised learning.

We also tokenize the weights, for example by grouping the parameters belonging to a neuron or a kernel into a token, and feed those sequences into a transformer-based autoencoder. Trained self-supervised with reconstruction and contrastive objectives, it learns what we call hyper-representations: a compact latent space that encodes the models.

What's exciting is what you can do with that space. You can predict properties of a model, like its accuracy, generalization gap, or which hyperparameters it was trained with, just by looking at its weights without running any data through it. And because it's an autoencoder, you can sample from the latent space and decode new weights, essentially generating models that serve as good initializations or even perform well out of the box.

So in short: build a diverse, well-documented population of models, respect the symmetries in weight space, tokenize sensibly, and learn representations self-supervised. That's how we turn weights into training data.

r001.rationale: The response describes grouping weights by neuron or kernel into tokens, but does not explain that this tokenization enables processing without relying on layer boundaries.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so this is really the core challenge of what we call weight space learning, or treating neural networks themselves as a data modality. The idea is simple to state: you take a population of trained models, and instead of looking at what they predict, you look at the weights directly and ask what the weights tell you about the model.

The first thing you run into is that weights are not like images or text. If you have a thousand small CNNs trained on CIFAR, every single one has a different initialization, a different training trajectory, maybe a different seed, and so the raw parameter vectors look wildly different even when the models behave almost identically. There are symmetries in there, permutation symmetries especially. You can swap two neurons in a hidden layer, rewire the next layer accordingly, and you get a functionally identical network with a completely different weight vector. So if you naively flatten the weights and feed them into a downstream model, you're asking it to learn something that is essentially invariant to a huge group of transformations, and that's hard.

So our approach has gone through a few stages. In the early work we built what we call model zoos, which are large, systematically generated populations of models where we control the generating factors, the architecture, the dataset, the hyperparameters, the seed. That gives you a clean dataset where you actually know the ground truth about each model. Then we trained what we called hyper-representations, essentially a self-supervised encoder over the flattened weights. We used contrastive objectives and reconstruction, and the key trick was to use augmentations that respect the symmetries, so permuting neurons, adding small noise, things that change the weights but not the function. The encoder then learns to be invariant to those, and the resulting embedding turns out to be surprisingly informative. You can predict test accuracy, generalization gap, what dataset the model was trained on, sometimes even hyperparameters, just from the embedding.

The second stage was dealing with scale and heterogeneity. Flattening works fine when all your models share one architecture, but in practice you want to process models of different sizes and shapes. So we moved to tokenizing the weights, treating each neuron or each slice of a layer as a token, adding positional information about where in the network it sits, and then using transformer style architectures over those tokens. That lets you handle different architectures in one model and also respects the structure much better than a flat vector.

And then there's the question of what you do with it. Once you have a representation of weights, you can go backwards, you can decode from the embedding back into weights. That's where it gets interesting, because now you can sample new models, you can do model generation, you can initialize a model in a good region of weight space instead of from random. We've shown you can get fine-tuned-quality initializations that train much faster, and you can transfer across tasks by moving in the embedding space.

So the short answer is: treat the population as the dataset, control the generating factors so you know what you're learning, build in the symmetries rather than hoping the model discovers them, and tokenize rather than flatten once you want to go across architectures.

r001.rationale: The response says weights are tokenized by neuron or layer slice and that this supports different architectures, but it does not state that processing can proceed without relying on layer boundaries.

astra-6.text:
We take the weights of a trained neural network and treat them as a data point. So instead of a dataset of images or text, we build a dataset of neural networks, and we learn a representation of their weights.

The tricky part is that weights aren’t aligned in the same way that pixels in an image are. You can permute the neurons in a layer, adjust the connections in the next layer accordingly, and still have exactly the same function. But if you simply flatten those weights into a vector, they look different. So we have to account for those symmetries when we train the representation.

A useful starting point is to work with models that share an architecture, because then their weight tensors have compatible shapes. We can break those weights into smaller pieces and encode them, rather than trying to process a whole network as one enormous vector. The objective is to capture meaningful properties of the model—what it has learned and how it behaves—rather than just the particular ordering of its parameters.

r001.rationale: The response says weights can be broken into smaller pieces and encoded, but does not explain that changing tokenization allows processing them without relying on layer boundaries.

sol-6.1.text:
We treat the weights of a neural network as a data point. Instead of training on images or text, we collect a population of trained networks and learn a representation of their weights.

The tricky part is that weights aren’t uniquely organized. Two networks can implement the same function while having their neurons in a different order. So simply flattening the weights and comparing them can be misleading. We need to account for those symmetries, as well as differences in scale across layers.

One approach is to break the weights into smaller pieces, embed those pieces, and train an encoder to capture the structure of the network. That representation can then support tasks like predicting model properties or generating new sets of weights. The important distinction is that we’re learning across a population of models, rather than looking at one model in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response says weights can be broken into smaller pieces and mentions layer-scale differences, but it does not explain that changing tokenization lets the model process weights without relying on layer boundaries.
